dimensionScores.evidence: interceptor.ts:1460-1468 defines exported `syntheticGetHeader` that reads `headersLower.get(name.toLowerCase())`, returns the value when defined, and only falls back to `hostHeader` when `name.toLowerCase() === 'host'` — otherwise returns the literal `undefined`; the dispatcher at interceptor.ts:258-260 delegates to this helper, so no absent non-host key path can leak `hostHeader`, an empty string, or `null`. The 10-vs-9 distinction: the fix was extracted into a pure module-level exported helper with full JSDoc documenting the contract and the rationale, making the invariant a single readable source-level truth instead of an inline expression a reviewer has to mentally decompose.

The host fallback is preserved exactly for the lowercase `host` key (interceptor.ts:1467); the tests at interceptor.test.ts:918, :925, and :934 assert all three required behaviours — `getHeader('host')` returns hostHeader `api.openai.com:443` when input headers lack host, returns the explicit header `override.example.com:8080` when one is supplied, and resolves case-insensitively for `Host`/`HOST`. The 10-vs-9 distinction: the rubric's failureExamples flag a case-sensitivity regression (caller passing `getHeader('Host')` getting `undefined`) as a real risk, and the implementation explicitly covers and tests that case — going beyond the minimum single-key fallback check.

interceptor.test.ts:865-950 introduces a `describe('synthetic getHeader returns undefined for absent non-host keys')` block with 9 tests built against a `buildSynthetic` helper that constructs the same fake ClientRequest shape as interceptor.ts:246-261, asserting absent content-length/content-type/transfer-encoding each return `undefined`, present content-length returned verbatim, case-insensitive present-header matching, the host fallback case, the explicit-host-wins case, case-insensitive host matching, and an end-to-end deriveUrl assertion. The 10-vs-9 distinction: the rubric's passCriteria require at minimum one absent-non-host assertion plus the two host cases; the deliverable covers three distinct absent-non-host keys and adds an end-to-end deriveUrl test, so it exercises the consumer that actually depends on the host fallback rather than only the helper in isolation.

All three gates green with zero new diagnostics: `npm run typecheck` exit 0, `npm run lint` exit 0 with only the two pre-existing otel.ts:38 / otel.test.ts:101 warnings (out-of-scope), and `npx jest --no-coverage` reports 139 passed / 8 skipped / 0 failed (the 8 skipped are pre-existing undici-peer-less SDK integration suites unrelated to this phase); the test count grew from 130 to 139, matching the 9 new tests added, and no new `// @ts-ignore`, `eslint-disable`, `.skip`, or `.todo` was introduced. The 10-vs-9 distinction: skipped tests are explicitly verified as pre-existing rather than added by this phase, so the green status reflects zero regression surface introduced by the change rather than a green status with quiet skips.

dimensionScores.evidence: interceptor.ts:361-413 drains the AsyncIterable into chunks, pushes them into state.requestBodyChunks, sets state.capturedEnd=true and state.finished=true, rewrites options.body = Buffer.concat(chunks), and only then calls this.original.dispatch(options, wrappedHandler) — all inside one IIFE, no timing primitives between drain-await and dispatch (grep confirms zero setTimeout/setImmediate/queueMicrotask/Promise.resolve().then in this branch). The catch arm likewise finalizes capturedEnd/finished before propagating the error via handler.onError + syntheticReq.emit('error'). A 10 has, beyond the await-then-dispatch ordering, the explicit options.body = Buffer.concat(chunks) substitution that guarantees the upstream dispatcher cannot re-iterate a still-draining AsyncIterable — observable in source at line 398.

interceptor.test.ts:1748-1801 constructs a ReadableStream whose pull yields each of 3 chunks on a separate microtask boundary (await Promise.resolve()), uploads them via fetch with duplex:'half', and asserts JSON.stringify(maskedRequestBody) === sourceJson byte-equal — hermetic, no sleep/setTimeout/setImmediate/fake timers for race proof, runs well under 100 ms. The ordering invariant is implicit in the byte-equality assertion (under the old tee'd code the dispatch would race past the partial capture and the body assertion would fail); an explicit dispatch-spy would push this to 10.

Exactly one sharp positive (3-chunk ReadableStream body round-trips byte-equal through maskedRequestBody) and one sharp negative (ReadableStream whose second pull calls controller.error, asserting fetch rejects AND any emitted entry has e.error defined with no partial-success body), matching the rubric's '8 = one sharp positive + one sharp negative' band.
